newsitem.title: USA: New storm compounds misery in U.S. Northwest.
newsitem.headline: New storm compounds misery in U.S. Northwest.

text.p: A new Pacific storm pounded the U.S. Northwest on Tuesday, compounding the misery of flood-hit Washington state and Oregon and raising fears of major flooding in northern California.

Washington Gov. Mike Lowry proclaimed a state of emergency in four more counties, bringing the number of Washington counties where emergencies have been declared to 19 since a series of punishing winter storms hit last week, causing widespread property damage, flooding and mudslides.
In Oregon, Jackson and Deschutes counties declared local emergencies due to the storms and asked the state for help.

The leading edge of a new storm dropped rain over the West coast on Tuesday but the full force of the storm was expected later on Tuesday evening and into New Year's Day, bringing more rain and wind gusts of up to 70 miles (110 kms) per hour.

The storms have caused 10 deaths since last week and an insurance industry group has estimated insured storm damage to businesses and homes in Washington state, Oregon and California at up to $250 million.
Rain and melting snow swelled dozens of rivers in western Washington state and Oregon to flood stage, inundating homes and streets in some areas.
The new storm was expected to worsen flooding and officials feared that the high winds in Washington state would bring down trees and power lines, cutting off power to more people.

About 445 evacuees spent Monday night in 16 shelters throughout Washington state, Lowry's office said, and more than 40,000 Washington residents remained without electricity, according to Puget Sound Power and Light Co.

Homes were flooded in Centralia, about 70 miles (110 km) south of Seattle, where a river burst its banks. Roofs of dozens of buildings in Washington and Oregon collapsed under the weight of snow and a mudslide in Mukilteo, near Seattle, swept seven homes off their foundations.
Mudslides and avalanches forced the closure of many highways throughout the western United States.
California, which has escaped relatively lightly so far from the storms, was expected to be hit hard by the approaching bad weather.

Local officials predicted "very heavy flooding" along the Russian River, 50 miles (80 kms) north of San Francisco, by New Year's Day and urged hundreds of local residents to evacuate before nightfall.

"Our fear is that residents will say it hasn't been raining that much and then will find tonight after dark that they need to leave," Janice Atkinson, a spokeswoman for the Sonoma County Office of Emergency Services, said.
By then, it would be dangerous to leave because it would be difficult to see flooded areas, she said.
"Roads are expected to become impassable after dark tonight. People should make plans to leave as soon as possible," she said.

Communities likely to be affected by the flooding included Guerneville and Monte Rio on the Russian River, she said. The Russian River was expected to peak at 45 feet (13.6 metres) at midnight on Tuesday at Guerneville, 13 feet (4 metres) above flood stage, she said.
The National Weather Service said the Napa River in northern California was also expected to rise above flood stage early on Wednesday morning.

The National Weather Service issued flood warnings for at least 10 rivers in Oregon, mostly in the west of the state. "It looks like the worst of the flooding will happen tomorrow and Thursday," Steve Todd, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Portland, said.
Many residents of Clackamas County, just south of Portland, Oregon, were sandbagging doorways to protect their homes from the rising waters of several rivers.
"There are some people that have water close enough to their homes that they've chosen to leave in various areas," said Casey Marley, emergency manager for Clackamas County.
"A lot of people have U-Hauls (moving vans) in their driveways to be ready to move out if the water continues to rise," she said.
